topStories.headline: Wasatch County Sheriff Goes on Paid Leave After Felony Indictment — Undersheriff to Take Charge
topStories.dek: The County Council unanimously accepted Sheriff Jared Rigby's offer to step back from daily duties while his obstruction-of-justice case moves through the courts.
topStories.body:
The Wasatch County Council voted unanimously on Wednesday, October 21, to formally place Sheriff Jared Rigby on voluntary paid administrative leave, ending a standoff that had threatened to produce a more dramatic confrontation. The council had been poised to vote on a resolution calling for Rigby's outright resignation, but on the eve of that meeting Rigby sent a letter to the council and County Manager Dustin Grabau saying he would step back from day-to-day duties voluntarily while his criminal case remains pending in Third District Court.

Rigby was indicted by a grand jury in September and pleaded not guilty on October 7 to one count of obstruction of justice — a second-degree felony — and one count of making a written false statement, a class B misdemeanor. Prosecutors allege he sent an anonymous letter containing false information aimed at interfering with a potential witness in the Kouri Richins murder trial. Because of the pending felony charge, state officials had already revoked Rigby's access to the Utah Criminal Justice Information System, severely limiting his ability to carry out core law-enforcement duties.

County officials had previously offered to pay Rigby the remainder of his salary and benefits in exchange for his resignation, an offer he declined. The council ultimately dropped the resignation resolution after Rigby's leave offer, which County Council Chair Erik Rowland described as making the resignation question moot. Under the arrangement, Undersheriff Josh Probst will lead the Sheriff's Office for the remainder of Rigby's term, which expires in January 2027.

Rigby lost his bid for a third term in the June Republican primary, defeated by Wasatch County Emergency Management Director Jeremy Hales, who will face write-in candidate Paul Moore in the November 3 general election. Rigby's departure from day-to-day duties removes a cloud of operational uncertainty that had hung over the department since the indictment.

topStories.headline: Indoor Pickleball Hall and a Possible Bypass Shift Come Before Heber City Council
topStories.dek: A developer wants to put indoor pickleball courts, a bank, and a coffee shop near Wasatch High School — and UDOT is studying whether the planned bypass road should swing further east.
topStories.body:
Heber City's October 20 council meeting covered two projects with long-term implications for the city's shape and character. Councilmember Morgan Murdock, who recapped the session for KPCW the following morning, said the council heard an early-stage presentation from developer Dave Johnson on a mixed-use project he is calling 'The Pickle Hall.' As currently envisioned, the development would place a bank and a coffee shop along Main Street, with indoor pickleball courts and additional amenities tucked behind on a lot near Wasatch High School.

Murdock described the conversation as exploratory, focused primarily on understanding questions about the property's relationship to nearby roadways rather than on formal approval. No vote was taken on the proposal at the October 20 meeting.

The council also discussed an amendment to Heber City's agreement with Wasatch County designed to strengthen protections for the North Fields — the agricultural buffer that both entities have long sought to preserve. Separately, Murdock noted that the Utah Department of Transportation is actively evaluating whether to shift the alignment of the long-planned Heber Valley bypass road eastward to reduce environmental impacts. The bypass has been a priority transportation project for the valley for years, and any realignment would affect where future development pressure falls along the corridor.

topStories.headline: Cyberattack Update: Systems Restored, FBI Forensic Work Continues
topStories.dek: Heber City's municipal network is fully back online after the October 10 breach, but the FBI's investigation into what data may have been exposed is still underway.
topStories.body:
City officials confirmed this week that Heber City's municipal IT systems have been fully restored following the October 10 cyberattack that breached the local government network. Mayor Heidi Franco and Police Chief Parker Sever said that police records, emergency dispatch, and the city website were unaffected throughout the incident, and that residents can continue using online bill pay and other services at heberut.gov with confidence.

Police records are stored on county servers and were never at risk, and the city website runs on a separate cloud-based platform. The city's IT team contained the intrusion quickly, and systems were reported back online within roughly a week of the attack. The FBI is now conducting a forensic review to determine the full scope of the breach, including whether any sensitive data was exposed. Officials said there is no concern about further spread, but the forensic investigation is expected to take additional time before a complete picture of the incident is available to the public.

moreNews.headline: Historic Crook Cabin Cleared for Installation Near School District Offices
moreNews.body: The 1859 Crook Cabin — the oldest known surviving example of a Heber Fort pioneer cabin — has cleared a key milestone on its way to a permanent public home. The Heber City Historic Preservation Commission reported at its July 20, 2026, meeting that Heber City had issued a building permit for the cabin's placement on a prepared pad near the Wasatch County School District office, adjacent to existing monuments including the Chief Tabby monument near 2nd North and 1st East. Commission Chair Ron Carlisle said the engineering and structural documentation needed for the permit had been completed, and that the project could proceed to site preparation and coordination with public works. Heber Valley Life reported in its October 20, 2026, issue that the cabin has since risen on site. The cabin was built inside the original Heber Fort by John Crook and his neighbors; Crook was among the valley's first settlers and served as its earliest chronicler.
moreNews.sourceName: CitizenPortal.ai (Heber City Historic Preservation Commission, July 20, 2026)

moreNews.headline: Wasatch County General Election Ballots Now in Mailboxes — Nov. 3 Deadline
moreNews.body: With the November 3 general election less than two weeks away, Wasatch County mail ballots have been sent to registered voters. The ballot includes races for three County Council seats, County Sheriff, County Attorney, Clerk-Auditor, two School Board seats, and Utah House District 59. The sheriff's race pits Republican primary winner Jeremy Hales against unaffiliated write-in candidate Paul Moore. For County Council Seat A, Rachel Kahler (R) faces Robert McNeill (D) and write-in candidates Jami Hewlett and Shawn Taylor; Seat C incumbent Erik Rowland (R) faces write-in Alex Folmer; and Seat F has Republican Mike Murphy against Democrat Joe Tugaw. Voters can verify registration and view a sample ballot at vote.utah.gov.
